lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you learnt about big feelings. What is one way to calm one? (Slow breaths, counting, moving, or talking to someone.) Today: mental health, and how to look after it.
Mental health is how we think and feel, and how we cope with life's ups and downs. Everyone has mental health, just as everyone has physical health, and it can change from day to day.
All feelings are normal, even uncomfortable ones like worry, anger and sadness. Feelings come and go. Noticing them and naming them is the first step to handling them.
Five ways to wellbeing, one for each finger: connect with people, be active, keep learning, give to others, and take notice of the world around you. Each helps your mind feel well.
Look after your mental health every day: sleep well, eat regular meals, move your body, spend time outdoors and with people you like, and take breaks from screens.
Sometimes feelings are very strong, last a long time, or stop you doing things you usually enjoy. That is the time to get help. Mental health problems are common, and they get better with help.
Talk to a trusted adult: family, a teacher or a school nurse. In the UK you can also call Childline, free, on 0800 1111, day or night. Asking for help is a strong and sensible thing to do.
Try it in the world: build a calm garden with a bench for taking notice, and invite a friend to sit there. For real: try one of the five ways to wellbeing each day this week. Next: stress and coping.

exercises.hint: Is it only some people who think and feel?
exercises.explain: True: everyone has mental health, just as everyone has physical health.

exercises.prompt: Which is one of the five ways to wellbeing?
exercises.hint: Which choice would help your mind and your body at the same time?
exercises.explain: Be active: moving helps your mind as well as your body.

exercises.hint: Are uncomfortable feelings part of life?
exercises.explain: True: all feelings are normal, and they come and go.

exercises.prompt: Who could you talk to if a feeling will not go away?
exercises.hint: Who keeps you safe and listens?
exercises.explain: A trusted adult, like family, a teacher or a school nurse.

exercises.prompt: Match each way to wellbeing to an example.
exercises.explain: Connect: chat with grandma. Be active: cycle. Give: help a neighbour. Take notice: listen to the birds.

exercises.prompt: Does it help your mental health?
exercises.hint: Think about sleep, food, people and moving.
exercises.explain: Helps: sleep, time outdoors, talking. Does not help: late screens, skipping meals, hiding every worry.

exercises.prompt: When is it time to get help with feelings?
exercises.hint: Think of how strong a feeling is and how long it lasts.
choices: when they are very strong or last a long time
only when you are grown up
exercises.explain: When feelings are very strong, last a long time or stop you enjoying things: talk to a trusted adult.

exercises.prompt: Mental health problems are rare and cannot get better.
exercises.hint: Think about how common they are, and what help does.
exercises.explain: False: they are common, and they get better with help.

exercises.prompt: What is Childline's free number in the UK?
exercises.hint: It starts 0800, like other free numbers.

exercises.prompt: Which way to wellbeing is learning to juggle?
exercises.hint: Which finger is about trying something new?
exercises.explain: Keep learning: trying a new skill.

exercises.prompt: Tilly has felt low for weeks and has stopped enjoying football. What is the best step?
exercises.hint: Strong feelings that last a long time are a sign to get help.
choices: tell a trusted adult how she feels
exercises.explain: Tell a trusted adult: feelings that last weeks and stop you enjoying things need help, and help works.

exercises.hint: Taking notice means paying attention to right now.
choices: tasting food slowly and noticing its flavour
exercises.explain: Tasting slowly: paying attention to the present moment.

exercises.prompt: Being physically active can help you feel better in your mind too.
exercises.hint: Think of how you feel after a walk or a game.
exercises.explain: True: moving lifts your mood and helps you sleep.

exercises.prompt: A friend seems upset. Put what you could do in order.
exercises.hint: First find out, then listen, then help them get support.
items: suggest they talk to a trusted adult
exercises.explain: Ask 'Are you OK?', listen, then suggest a trusted adult.

exercises.prompt: Why is asking for help a strong thing to do?
exercises.hint: What happens after someone asks for help?
choices: it takes courage, and it helps things get better
so you never feel anything again
exercises.explain: It takes courage, and it is the first step to feeling better.

items: join a club and meet people
make a card for someone ill
say thank you to the dinner staff
exercises.hint: People, moving, or doing something kind?
exercises.explain: Connect: a club, phoning a friend. Be active: walking the dog, dancing. Give: a card, saying thank you.

exercises.prompt: Match each habit to how it helps your mind.
matches: fresh air and daylight lift mood
more time for people and play
exercises.hint: Each habit looks after your mind in a different way.
exercises.explain: Sleep lets your brain rest and recharge. Time outdoors gives fresh air and daylight. Screen breaks leave time for people and play. Talking makes a worry feel smaller.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a feeling to notice and handle, or a sign it is time to get help?
items: sad for a day after a goodbye
worries that stop you sleeping for weeks
exercises.hint: Help is needed when feelings are very strong, last a long time, or stop you enjoying things.
exercises.explain: Handle: nerves before a test, being cross after a game and a sad day after a goodbye come and go. Get help: feeling low for weeks, losing all enjoyment and weeks of lost sleep: talk to a trusted adult.
